title: 3 Types of Investors Who Should Avoid SpaceX and Tesla Stocks as the Companies Explore a Potential Merger

3 Types of Investors Who Should Avoid SpaceX and Tesla Stocks as the Companies Explore a Potential Merger
Will Healy, The Motley Fool

TSLA
NVDA

Trading disclosure

On Space Exploration Technologies' (NASDAQ: SPCX) third-quarter earnings call on Oct. 20, CEO Elon Musk revealed that the company and his other megacap, Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA), are contemplating a merger.

Not surprisingly, many investors have taken a strong interest in a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger. The combined entity would be one of the world's largest AI companies.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Although many investors would likely own stakes in that company, such a stock is not suitable for everyone. In particular, these three types of investors should probably not rush to buy it.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
1. Novice investors

Even for those who know nothing about investing, both SpaceX and Tesla might look like attractive choices on the surface. Both are growing their revenues thanks to technologies that increasingly interest the public, and Musk's past successes add to their appeal.

However, most investors do not own individual stocks. Instead, they tend to own long-term passive mutual funds and exchange-traded funds held in their retirement accounts. That is a sensible strategy, particularly for investors who don't have the time or willingness to dig into the details of individual businesses' competitive advantages, risks, and financial metrics. Many of these funds may include Tesla and SpaceX among their numerous other holdings.

Moreover, if one wants to learn how to invest in stocks, most experts recommend starting with companies that have well-known brands, solid balance sheets, and long track records. SpaceX and Tesla are both well-known, but SpaceX doesn't even have a full year under its belt as a public company, and Tesla only went public in 2010 -- that's not a terribly long track record either.

Moreover, objectively speaking, these companies' financials may not be the easiest to understand. Blue chips such as Home Depot or Chevron, which have existed for decades and operate in more straightforward businesses, may make better sense as one's first stock picks.

2. Risk-averse investors

Another aspect of investing that both novices and veterans alike must account for in their choices is their risk tolerance.

Risk-averse investors would rather accept less growth potential in exchange for a lower chance that they'll actually lose money on a stock. As such, they are better advised to buy slower-growing stocks in stable businesses that are less likely to fall in the long run. Even in bear markets, they tend to decline less than cutting-edge tech companies that get valued heavily on the future potential, and those slow-and-steady stocks often pay dividends.

title: Tesla's Q3 Per-Car Fiscal Metrics Show Minor but Important Progress
detail:
Tesla's Q3 Per-Car Fiscal Metrics Show Minor but Important Progress
James Brumley, The Motley Fool
Tue, October 27, 2026 at 8:36 AM MST 4 min read
TSLA
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tesla's (NASDAQ: TSLA) recently reported quarterly results raise as many questions as they answer. While revenue of just over $28 billion topped estimates of $27.9 billion, and earnings of $0.48 per share beat estimates of $0.43, investors apparently balked at the company's 2026 spending outlook.

Not because it was raised, but because it was lowered, from around $25 billion to $20 billion, and will largely be funded from operating cash flow. The market is interpreting that as a sign that Tesla's transition to predominantly an artificial intelligence (AI) technology company isn't happening very quickly. And maybe that's an accurate assessment.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

In the meantime, though, Tesla remains first and foremost an electric vehicle (EV) company that's using that business's bottom line as a springboard for its AI-driven robotaxi and robotics ventures. And we're seeing encouraging progress on the electric vehicle front, not so much in terms of volume, but at least in terms of profitability.

When it was needed the most, a small step forward

Whether Tesla's EV business is a meaningfully reliable growth engine has been up for debate since 2022, when Chinese rival BYD Company (OTC: BYDDY) began getting real traction in China as well as in Europe. Tesla cut prices, which, of course, crimped profits.

There's a glimmer of hope, though. While average selling prices have dropped since the first quarter -- partially reflecting more sales and production of the lower-cost Model 3 -- the latest numbers show that for the second quarter in a row, Tesla's per-car production costs have fallen as well, from $37,748 in Q2 to Q3's $36,077.

This has allowed per-delivery automotive gross profits to bounce back from Q2's plunge to $7,213 to $7,864 in Q3. Gross profits per manufactured vehicle also snapped back by a similar degree, negating any worries that the recovery is merely a matter of the difference between the quarter's delivery figure and its production tally.

Data source: Tesla. Chart by author.
Just buying stress-free time

This isn't necessarily thrilling. As the graphic above illustrates, per-car profits are far from soaring.

They're not sinking, though, and that's a win in and of itself following a concerning decline in Q2. This slight recovery confirms there's at least some degree of profitable marketability for Tesla's electric vehicles in an increasingly competitive environment.

Anthropic's planned IPO has reignited interest in the sector (SEBASTIEN BOZON)

Tech firms rose Tuesday for a second day as AI titan Anthropic's IPO filing revived optimism over the sector.

But gains were tempered as traders awaited key earnings reports and central bank meetings.

In New York, the tech-heavy Nasdaq led the way, up more than one percent in midday trading. The wider S&P 500 was also higher, but not by as much, while the Dow was little changed.

In a share-launch filing Monday, Anthropic, the mother company for Claude AI, reported first-half revenue surged about 1,300 percent year-on-year, but also flagged heavy capital spending ahead.

"The fact that this five year-old company could soon launch a record-breaking IPO helped boost investor confidence, following a decidedly rocky period across AI-adjacent corporations of late," said David Morrison, an analyst at Trade Nation.

Tesla, Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft were all trading higher.

In London, the benchmark FTSE 100 index was dragged down by HSBC, whose share price fell 5.4 percent after its bumper profits undershot market expectations.

Mercedes-Benz shed 3.8 percent in Frankfurt after the German carmaker cut its full-year outlook, underperforming the DAX index which slightly rose overall in afternoon trading. Paris also rose.

Earlier, equities rose in Japan and Korea, also boosted by Anthropic's IPO filing.

The sale is seen as a crucial test of whether the AI boom can deliver profits, and a disappointing reception could dent enthusiasm further, with traders questioning the vast sums invested in the sector as well as several companies' financial positions.

The filing lays out risks for the AI industry, which has faced a string of damaging reports in recent months.

Seoul's stock market briefly jumped more than four percent Tuesday thanks to strong gains in chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung.

Tokyo added 1.8 percent on spikes in Tokyo Electron, Advantest and SoftBank.

"Sentiment towards technology has improved as investors assess Anthropic's IPO filing at the start of a week packed with corporate earnings and the Federal Reserve's rate decision," said Fiona Cincotta at FOREX.com.

IG analyst Chris Beauchamp said "there remains hope that this is a more durable rally than those we saw last week, with the caveat that there is still an abundance of macro risk to navigate this week."

Investors are awaiting earnings this week from Magnificent Seven members Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon as well as SK hynix and Samsung.

Facebook parent Meta on Monday said it plans to raise $35 billion through a stock offering to fund artificial intelligence development.

PrimeXBT Adds Seven Tokenized Stock Crypto Futures, Including Tesla, SpaceX and Nvidia

PrimeXBT, a crypto and multi-asset broker, has launched a new category of crypto futures linked to the prices of seven major publicly traded companies, including Tesla (NASDAQ: $TSLA), SpaceX (NASDAQ: $SPCX) and Nvidia (NASDAQ: $NVDA), the company announced Tuesday.

The product, called Tokenised Stocks, runs on the broker's PXTrader 2.0 platform. It includes USDT-denominated futures tied to SpaceX, Nvidia, Tesla, Circle (NYSE: $CRCL), Apple (NASDAQ: $AAPL), Alphabet (NASDAQ: $GOOGL) and Robinhood (NASDAQ: $HOOD). Traders can take long or short positions around the clock, including outside regular stock market hours. The contracts give exposure to price movements without ownership of the underlying shares, PrimeXBT said.

That makes them derivatives, not tokenized shares of the kind that platforms such as OKXICE are seeking to list, an effort that more than 20 companies have objected to.
